profile.summary: This is the in silico cyclic peptide design comparison published with TorchCraft. Eight target systems, listed with PDB entries, crops, hotspots and a peptide length range of 12 to 18 residues in Supplementary Table S6, are designed against by BoltzGen, RFpeptides and TorchCraft, with 100 designs per method per target in the head-to-tail cyclisation setting; TorchCraft is also run in a disulfide-linked setting. A design passes only if its predicted structure forms the intended cycle without chain breaks and its TorchScore pLDDT exceeds 70 and ipTM exceeds 0.5. Figure 4c prints the pass rates per target. The question it answers is which design method produces cyclic peptides that satisfy both the cyclisation geometry and a confidence threshold.
profile.summary_source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4 and Figure 4c; Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Table S6

summary_quotes.text: We compared cyclic-peptide designs for eight target systems with outputs from RFpeptides and BoltzGen using the structural and confidence criteria defined in Appendix A.4 (Figure 4c). Performance depended on both the target and cyclization mode. Disulfide-linked TorchCraft designs showed higher computational pass rates in several settings, including PD-L1 and GABARAP, whereas head-to-tail designs displayed a different target-dependent profile. Optional ProteinMPNN redesign improved pass rates in several comparisons.
A cyclic-peptide design passed the computational criterion only if the predicted structure formed the intended cycle without chain breaks and satisfied TorchScore pLDDT > 70 and ipTM > 0.5.
In the head-to-tail cyclization benchmark, each method generated 100 designs per target using its default settings.

sections.title: What it measures
sections.body: Two things at once, which is what makes this panel different from the others: whether the predicted peptide is actually cyclic and intact, and whether the predictor is confident about the complex. The authors evaluate two cyclisation parameterisations, head-to-tail, which uses cyclic relative positional encoding so the termini are adjacent in sequence space, and disulfide-linked, which keeps linear encoding and fixes the two cysteine positions that define the linkage. Predicted structures are classified by whether they satisfy the intended cyclisation and the backbone-integrity criteria, with the breakdown of cyclised, intact but not cyclised and backbone-broken predictions reported in a supplementary figure.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Section 2.4; Supplementary Figure S6 caption

quotes.text: We next evaluated cyclic-peptide design computationally using two parameterizations (Figure 4a). Head-to-tail designs used cyclic relative positional encoding to represent sequence adjacency across the termini. Disulfide- linked designs retained linear positional encoding and fixed the cysteine positions defining the intended linkage.

Figure S6 Cyclization outcomes for cyclic-peptide designs. Fractions of successfully cyclized, intact-but- not-cyclized, and backbone-broken predictions across cyclic-peptide benchmark targets for the head-to-tail and disulfide-linked TorchCraft settings.

sections.title: How it is built
sections.body: A target panel, not a dataset, and no split. Supplementary Table S6 lists eight target systems with a PDB entry, the target chains and residue crop, hotspot residues and a peptide length of 12 to 18 residues for each: MDM2, MCL-1, GABARAP, PD-L1, KEAP1, RagA:RagC, IL-23R and albumin, counted from its rows. In the head-to-tail benchmark each method generates 100 designs per target with its default settings. TorchCraft is additionally evaluated in the disulfide-linked setting, where all positions except the two cysteines may be redesigned in the polished variant.

For head-to-tail TorchCraft outputs, we evaluated raw designs scored directly with TorchScore and an optional ProteinMPNN-polished variant in which all peptide positions were redesigned eight times; the subsequent FlowPacker and TorchScore selection procedure was identical to that used for BoltzGen and RFpeptides. TorchCraft was also evaluated in a disulfide-linked cyclization setting. For this setting, raw outputs were scored directly, or all positions except the two cysteines were redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN, followed by the same FlowPacker rebuilding and TorchScore selection protocol used for the head-to-tail setting.

sections.title: Evaluation methodology
sections.body: For BoltzGen and RFpeptides the full peptide sequence of each generated structure is redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN without fixing residues, each redesign is rebuilt with FlowPacker and scored with TorchScore, and the redesign with the highest pLDDT plus 100 times ipTM becomes that original design's score. TorchCraft head-to-tail outputs are scored raw and, optionally, after redesigning all peptide positions eight times with the same rebuild and selection procedure. In the disulfide-linked setting raw outputs are scored directly, or all positions except the two cysteines are redesigned eight times and then rebuilt and selected in the same way. The pass criterion has three parts that must all hold: the intended cycle must be formed, the backbone must have no chain breaks, and TorchScore pLDDT must exceed 70 with ipTM above 0.5. Rosetta interface scores for the same panel are reported separately as an orthogonal assessment.
sections.source_locator: Paper: Appendix A.4.3.3; Supplementary Figure S7 caption

quotes.text: For cyclic-peptide design, we compared BoltzGen, RFpeptides, and TorchCraft. In the head-to-tail cyclization benchmark, each method generated 100 designs per target using its default settings. For BoltzGen and RFpeptides, the full peptide sequence of each generated structure was redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN without fixing any residue. Each redesigned sequence was rebuilt with FlowPacker, scored with TorchScore, and the redesign with the highest pLDDT + 100 × ipTM was selected as the final structure and score for that original design.

For head-to-tail TorchCraft outputs, we evaluated raw designs scored directly with TorchScore and an optional ProteinMPNN-polished variant in which all peptide positions were redesigned eight times; the subsequent FlowPacker and TorchScore selection procedure was identical to that used for BoltzGen and RFpeptides. TorchCraft was also evaluated in a disulfide-linked cyclization setting. For this setting, raw outputs were scored directly, or all positions except the two cysteines were redesigned eight times with ProteinMPNN, followed by the same FlowPacker rebuilding and TorchScore selection protocol used for the head-to-tail setting.
A cyclic-peptide design passed the computational criterion only if the predicted structure formed the intended cycle without chain breaks and satisfied TorchScore pLDDT > 70 and ipTM > 0.5.

Figure S7 Rosetta interface-score benchmark for cyclic-peptide designs. The cyclic-peptide benchmark from Figure 4c evaluated using Rosetta interface score as an orthogonal assessment of predicted target-binding quality.

sections.title: What TorchScore is
sections.body: The scorer every pass rate in this panel depends on is worth stating plainly, because it is not an independent evaluator. TorchScore is a score-only loading of the same TorchFold implementation used for design: given input coordinates it skips the diffusion structure module and runs the confidence pathway, returning pLDDT, pTM and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained, and in this study it used the pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights, the same checkpoint the designs were optimised against. Sequences rebuilt with FlowPacker are scored from those coordinates and are not refolded from sequence.

quotes.text: TorchScore is a score-only loading of the TorchFold implementation.[21] Given input coordinates, it bypasses the diffusion-based structure module and evaluates the complex through the confidence pathway, returning predictor-derived scores including pLDDT, pTM, and ipTM. No separate scoring network is trained.

In this study, TorchScore used pretrained AF3 weights, the same checkpoint used for design. Designed sequences that were rebuilt with FlowPacker were scored from the resulting coordinates; they were not refolded from sequence by TorchScore.

facts.label: Leakage controls
facts.value: None, and none is needed in the train and test sense: no model is trained here and the panel has no labels to hold out. What the sources do describe is a dependency that runs the other way, which the authors state plainly: TorchScore uses the same pretrained AlphaFold 3 weights that TorchCraft optimised against, so the scorer is not independent of the designer.

review.note: Written from the pdftotext -layout text layer of arXiv:2609.19770v1 and from the README and LICENSE of Mingchenchen/TorchX at commit ebf9dc6676ecb1be505bc72f87de408995f0d8fd, all retrieved 27 November 2026. The main text, the figure caption, Appendix A.4.2 and A.4.3 and the supplementary target table were read directly. Nothing was reproduced: no design was generated and no score was recomputed. No human review is claimed.

no_run_guide_reason: No scoring harness for this panel is published. The code repository the paper names holds the design and score entry points, but nothing that reproduces the figure's pass rates from a set of designs, and the target crops and hotspots live in supplementary tables rather than in a machine-readable manifest.
